The natural next move is to klaus (2019) end-to-end. Once Klaus (2019) clicks, the rest of film feels more connected.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film as a story about how kindness spreads — every act of generosity in the town creates another. Then notice the film's animation: the hand-drawn style with volumetric lighting is the film's quiet revolution.

name: The Gentlemen (2019)
teaser: Guy Ritchie's return to his London crime-comedy roots was praised for its cast and its storytelling — Matthew McConaughey leads a tale of a weed empire being sold. The film's framing device, a journalist's pitch, is the joke. You meet The Gentlemen (2019) early in film — keep Crime in mind from the start. It matters more than it looks: The Gentlemen (2019) sits under a surprising amount of film. It shows up in Comedy: once you know what to look for, you notice it constantly. A good way in: The Gentlemen (2019) end-to-end. That is the kind of understanding that shows up again and again in film.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film as a story about the performance of power — every character is trying to look like the one in charge. Then notice the film's structure: the narrator's version of events is the film's unreliability.

name: And Then There Were None (1945)
teaser: Ten strangers are lured to a remote island mansion, and one by one they die according to a nursery rhyme. Agatha Christie's best-selling novel, adapted faithfully by René Clair, turns the mystery into a tight, elegant thriller. The killer is one of the ten — and the film lets you suspect all of them. A perfect locked-room puzzle.

exploreAction.targetName: And Then There Were None (1945) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how Clair withholds the identity of the killer. Notice the rhythm: each death follows the rhyme, and every survivor's alibi collapses under the next accusation.

name: The Big Heat (1953)
teaser: A police detective refuses to drop a case and watches his world collapse around him — his wife murdered, his badge tarnished. Fritz Lang's brutal noir tracks his slow, cold descent into vengeance. Gloria Grahame's scalding-coffee scene is among the most shocking moments of 1950s cinema.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how Lang films violence as aftermath rather than spectacle. Notice that the hero's quest for justice slowly becomes indistinguishable from the crime.

name: The Umbrellas of Cherbourg (1964)
teaser: A young woman and a garage mechanic fall in love, are separated by war and money, and drift apart in a small French port — every line of dialogue sung. Jacques Demy's opera-film is drenched in candy colors and unbearable tenderness. Its final scene, a filling-station conversation, is one of cinema's great heartbreaking goodbyes.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the colors — every set, dress and wall is a deliberate shade of the palette. Notice that because everyone sings, the sadness arrives without warning.

name: For a Few Dollars More (1965)
teaser: Two bounty hunters — one elegant, one feral — agree to split the reward on a sadistic bank robber, while each plans to cheat the other. Sergio Leone's second western sharpened the formula before the trilogy peaked. The twin timepieces, the waltz, and the Man with No Name made violence into choreography.

exploreAction.targetName: For a Few Dollars More (1965) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the mirror duel between Lee Van Cleef and Clint Eastwood in the opening. Notice how Leone builds every shootout as a musical piece — the silence before the gunfire is the song.

name: Pat Garrett and Billy the Kid (1973)
teaser: An aging sheriff is ordered to hunt down the outlaw he once rode with, and the two old friends play out their last act in a dying West. Sam Peckinpah's elegy was cut by the studio and later restored — both versions worth seeing. Bob Dylan's score, especially 'Knockin' on Heaven's Door', carries the sadness.

exploreAction.targetName: Pat Garrett and Billy the Kid (1973) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the scenes of Garrett and Billy together — the friendship is the film's center. Notice how the film keeps returning to rivers, the West's version of time passing.

name: The Killing of a Chinese Bookie (1976)
teaser: A strip-club owner owes a gambling debt he cannot pay, and the mob offers him one job: kill the owner of a rival club. John Cassavetes' raw, meandering crime film is less a heist than a portrait of a man improvising his own ruin. The title is a lie that makes the film truer.

exploreAction.targetName: The Killing of a Chinese Bookie (1976) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the club sequences — the musical numbers are the film's heart. Notice how Cassavetes lets scenes run past their point, the way real dread does.

name: Suspiria (1977)
teaser: An American dancer arrives at a prestigious German ballet academy and discovers it is run by a coven of witches. Dario Argento's horror opera is a symphony of saturated color, Goblin's pulsing score and set-piece violence. Plot is beside the point; the nightmare is the film.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — a taxi in a storm, a door, and a murder within minutes. Notice how Argento lights every set in primary colors; the film is a painting that happens to move.

name: The Passion of Joan of Arc (1928)
teaser: Joan of Arc is interrogated, condemned and burned — and the film is almost entirely her face. Carl Theodor Dreyer shot the trial in close-up on white sets, with Renée Falconetti's transcendent performance. The camera barely moves; the emotion does all the moving. It is often called the greatest performance ever filmed.

exploreAction.targetName: The Passion of Joan of Arc (1928) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch Falconetti's face — the film's entire drama is there. Notice how Dreyer strips away everything until only suffering, and then grace, remains.

name: Vampyr (1932)
teaser: A young man drifts into a village where the dead do not stay dead, and dreams and reality blur into one fog. Carl Theodor Dreyer's horror film is less a vampire story than a nightmare photographed. The shadow-play, the coffin sequence and the scythe-carrying ghost make it the most beautiful horror film ever made.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the scene filmed as if through the eyes of the buried — the film's most famous trick. Notice how Dreyer keeps everything in soft focus, like a memory you can't quite reach.

name: Grand Illusion (1937)
teaser: French officers in a German POW camp plot escape while their aristocratic captor and a Jewish banker argue about class across the trenches. Jean Renoir's anti-war film is a tragedy about the things that unite men — and the borders that divide them. The word 'illusion' is the thesis: the old certainties were already dying.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the shared meal between the French aristocrat and the German commandant — the film's center. Notice how the escapes matter less than the bonds formed in between.

name: His Girl Friday (1940)
teaser: A newspaper editor will do anything — even pretend to be divorced — to keep his best reporter, who also happens to be his ex-wife, from quitting to marry a dull insurance man. Howard Hawks' screwball masterpiece fires dialogue like a machine gun and never lets up. The famous 'faster' pacing made it the fastest comedy ever made.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the overlapping dialogue — everyone talks over everyone, and the film is funnier for it. Notice that the love story is conducted entirely through newsroom warfare.

name: The Philadelphia Story (1940)
teaser: A heiress's second wedding is crashed by a gossip magazine and the ex-husband who sold the story. George Cukor's drawing-room comedy brings Katharine Hepburn, Cary Grant and James Stewart together for the greatest screwball triangle ever. Stewart won his only Oscar as the soaked reporter who sees through her.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch Hepburn's entrance — a star being introduced to her public. Notice how the film's drunk scene lets everyone speak the truth they soberly avoid.

name: The Lady Eve (1941)
teaser: A con woman sets out to fleece a rich, shy snake expert — and falls for him instead, then exacts a hilarious revenge when he rejects her. Preston Sturges' comedy is the purest screwball ever made, with Barbara Stanwyck and Henry Fonda at their peak. The final reunion, complete with snakes and slapstick, is perfection.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch Stanwyck's two performances as two different women — one good, one very good at being bad. Notice how the film keeps inventing new ways to make embarrassment hilarious.

name: The Magnificent Ambersons (1942)
teaser: A spoiled family in turn-of-the-century Indianapolis watches the automobile and the modern world erase their grand estate. Orson Welles' second film was cut and re-shot by the studio — but even the mutilated version is a masterpiece. The ballroom sequence alone justifies its legend.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the sleigh-ride montage — a whole era passing in a few minutes of cross-fades. Notice how the film mourns the Ambersons even while showing why they deserve to fall.

name: The Ox-Bow Incident (1943)
teaser: A posse lynches three innocent men for a murder they did not commit, and the discovery comes too late. William A. Wellman's western is a moral experiment about mob justice, filmed with a documentary's cold eye. Henry Fonda's helpless rage at the end is the film's verdict on the American frontier.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the lynching scene — no music, no heroics, just men doing a terrible thing carefully. Notice how the film refuses to let the audience feel clean.

name: The Lost Weekend (1945)
teaser: A writer's five-day bender becomes a tour of alcoholism's anatomy — the hidden bottles, the pawned typewriter, the lies told to everyone who loves him. Billy Wilder's film was the first major Hollywood movie to treat addiction as a disease. Ray Milland's performance earned him the Oscar, and the film earned the subject its dignity.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the hallucination sequence in the jazz club — delirium filmed from the inside. Notice how Wilder never lets the film become a lecture; it stays inside one man's desperate day.

name: The Postman Always Rings Twice (1946)
teaser: A drifter and a diner owner's wife plot to kill her husband, and the murder unravels them from the inside out. Tay Garnett's noir, from James M. Cain's novel, is built on heat, lust and a guilt that keeps resurfacing. The courtroom scenes made the film's title a byword for fate's second knock.

exploreAction.targetName: The Postman Always Rings Twice (1946) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the first kiss — a scene so charged it forced the studio to rewrite the script. Notice how every attempt to escape the crime only tightens its hold.

name: The Big Sleep (1946)
teaser: Private eye Philip Marlowe is hired to handle a blackmailer and ends up wading through a swamp of gambling debts, pornography and murder. Howard Hawks' adaptation of Raymond Chandler is the loosest of great noirs — the plot is famously tangled, and nobody cares. Bogart and Bacall's chemistry carries it past every puzzle.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the chemistry — the film is really a flirtation disguised as a mystery. Notice how the plot's loose ends are the point: Chandler's world is a fog with moments of clarity.

name: Letter from an Unknown Woman (1948)
teaser: A pianist receives a letter from a woman he never really noticed — she loved him her whole life, and now she is writing to him one last time. Max Ophüls' melodrama is a masterwork of longing told in a single act of reading. Joan Fontaine's devotion is the film's ache, and its indictment of the man who ignored it.

exploreAction.targetName: Letter from an Unknown Woman (1948) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the staircase scenes — Ophüls moves the camera up and down in swoops of feeling. Notice how the film lets you love the woman and judge the man in the same breath.

name: Ace in the Hole (1951)
teaser: A cynical reporter trapped in Albuquerque sees a man trapped in a cave as his ticket back to the big time — and keeps him trapped. Billy Wilder's darkest satire attacks the news media's hunger for tragedy. Kirk Douglas' Chuck Tatum is one of cinema's great monsters: charming, brilliant, and perfectly willing to let a man die for a headline.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the crowd at the cave becomes a carnival — the film's real subject. Notice that Tatum's schemes keep succeeding until they succeed too well.

name: The Day the Earth Stood Still (1951)
teaser: A visitor from space lands in Washington with a robot and a message: stop your wars, or be removed from the Earth's equation. Robert Wise's sci-fi classic made the alien a moral witness rather than a monster. Michael Rennie's Klaatu and the line 'Klaatu barada nikto' entered the language forever.

exploreAction.targetName: The Day the Earth Stood Still (1951) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the landing in the park — the crowd's fear of the unknown, staged with military precision. Notice how the film's alien is the one sane voice in a world of armies.

name: The Earrings of Madame de... (1953)
teaser: A general's wife pawns her earrings to pay a debt, and the earrings pass from hand to hand, returning to everyone who thought they were rid of them. Max Ophüls' chamber masterpiece is a waltz of objects, appearances and regret. The final ball, all glitter and grief, is among the greatest finales in cinema.

exploreAction.targetName: The Earrings of Madame de... (1953) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the camera — Ophüls glides through rooms and dances in one unbroken movement. Notice how the earrings' journey becomes the story of a marriage.

name: Sansho the Bailiff (1954)
teaser: A governor's children are sold into slavery when their father refuses to torture his people, and they grow up under a brutal bailiff — until the daughter finds a way to free them. Kenji Mizoguchi's folktale is a parable of mercy in a merciless world. Its ending, after years of cruelty, is one of cinema's great releases of light.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the mother's scene on the beach — a moment of unbearable longing. Notice how Mizoguchi films suffering without ever making it a spectacle.

name: La Strada (1954)
teaser: A strongman buys a simple girl to be his assistant, and their life on the road is a study in cruelty slowly waking into love. Federico Fellini's breakthrough made Giulietta Masina's Gelsomina one of cinema's great innocent souls. The ending, a man weeping by the sea, is the film's terrible epiphany.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch Gelsomina's trumpet and the clown's kindness — the film's two consolations. Notice how the strongman's violence is never justified, only understood.

name: Smiles of a Summer Night (1955)
teaser: A wealthy lawyer, his young bride, his old mistress and a theatre actress spend a weekend in the country untangling a dozen mismatched desires. Ingmar Bergman's first comedy is a carousel of couples swapping partners under the midnight sun. The famous final scene, the servant's wink, is cinema's most perfect comic punctuation.

exploreAction.targetName: Smiles of a Summer Night (1955) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the dinner scene — a round of confessions that rearranges every pairing. Notice how Bergman keeps the comedy light while the stakes stay painfully real.

name: Nights of Cabiria (1957)
teaser: A streetwalker with a heart of gold is robbed, humiliated and nearly drowned — and still believes in love. Federico Fellini's film is Giulietta Masina's masterpiece, a portrait of resilience that ends in tears turning to a smile. The final walk toward the camera is among cinema's most human moments.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the ending — Cabiria is betrayed and still walks toward the music. Notice how Fellini films her despair and her hope with the same tenderness.

name: The Cranes Are Flying (1957)
teaser: A young couple is torn apart by war — she gives birth to another man's child, he returns a different person — and the cranes pass overhead, indifferent. Mikhail Kalatozov's Soviet melodrama is famous for its virtuoso camera work, especially the staircase and the farewell at the front. It won the Palme d'Or and made grief a spectacle of motion.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — a crane shot that sweeps over the lovers as the city wakes. Notice how the camera becomes a character, moving with the emotion.

name: Pickpocket (1959)
teaser: A young man in Paris convinces himself that stealing is a superior form of living — and practices his craft until the craft practices on him. Robert Bresson's austere film is less a crime story than a spiritual exercise. The final scene, hands through the bars, is a redemption that arrives in silence.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the theft sequences — choreographed with ballet precision, hands as the only actors. Notice how Bresson strips acting away until only gesture and grace remain.

name: Black Orpheus (1959)
teaser: The Orpheus myth is retold during Carnival in Rio: a streetcar conductor loses his Eurydice, then descends into the city's underworld to find her. Marcel Camus' film won the Palme d'Or and introduced bossa nova to the world. The music, the color and the samba make the tragedy dance.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the Carnival scenes — the film's real content is the rhythm. Notice how the myth is updated but never diluted: the lovers are still doomed by the world's noise.

name: Eyes Without a Face (1960)
teaser: A brilliant surgeon kidnaps young women to transplant their faces onto his disfigured daughter — and the horror is almost tender. Georges Franju's French classic is both a gothic nightmare and an elegy. The famous mask, the white corridors and the piano score make it the most beautiful horror film of its era.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the surgery scene — clinical, poetic, and somehow gentle. Notice how the film's real horror is the father's devotion, not the knife.

name: La Jetée (1962)
teaser: A man haunted by a childhood memory is sent through time to save a post-war world — told entirely in still photographs, one of which moves. Chris Marker's 28-minute film is a science-fiction poem about memory and death. It directly inspired Terry Gilliam's Twelve Monkeys, but nothing matches its dreamlike compression.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the single moving image — the one moment the photographs surrender to film. Notice how the stills make every frame a memory, which is exactly the story.

name: The Leopard (1963)
teaser: An aging Sicilian prince watches the revolution of 1860 sweep away his class, and chooses to swim with the new tide — marrying his nephew to a merchant's daughter. Luchino Visconti's epic is a lament for aristocracy filmed in gold and candlelight. The final ball, an hour of dancing toward extinction, is cinema's greatest party.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the ballroom sequence — the film's entire argument in one endless dance. Notice how the prince's famous line, 'everything must change so that everything can stay the same', is both cynical and true.

name: High and Low (1963)
teaser: A wealthy executive must choose between his fortune and his chauffeur's son, kidnapped in a case of mistaken identity. Akira Kurosawa's thriller splits into two halves — the agonizing negotiation, then a detective's procedural manhunt — and both are perfect. The final confrontation through train windows is a masterclass in editing.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the first half, confined to one room, versus the second half's city-wide pursuit. Notice how Kurosawa turns a moral dilemma into a thriller without ever dropping the question.

name: Andrei Rublev (1966)
teaser: A medieval icon painter witnesses the brutality of his age — Tartar raids, torture, the making of a bell — and falls silent, until an act of creation brings him back. Andrei Tarkovsky's epic is a portrait of the artist under history's weight. The final images of Rublev's actual icons are a revelation.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the bell-casting finale — a masterpiece of physical cinema about faith in craft. Notice how Tarkovsky films violence as history's weather, not as spectacle.

name: PlayTime (1967)
teaser: A tourist in a Paris of glass and chrome wanders through a city that has become an airport terminal — and the film has almost no plot, only geometry. Jacques Tati's comedy is a utopia of sight gags built over years of meticulous staging. The restaurant collapse at the end is the greatest comedy sequence ever filmed.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the frame — every shot is a composition with jokes hidden in the corners. Notice how the film's 'plot' is just the excuse for the city to reveal itself.

name: Au Hasard Balthazar (1966)
teaser: A donkey is passed from owner to owner, and each passage marks another stage in a village's cruelty and grace. Robert Bresson's film is a parable without preaching — Balthazar's suffering mirrors a girl's, and both are witnessed by a camera that never flinches. The final scene, bells tolling for a dying donkey, is one of cinema's great religious moments.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch Balthazar's eyes — the film asks you to see through them without anthropomorphizing. Notice how every human in the film is also a beast, and the beast is also a saint.

name: Weekend (1967)
teaser: A couple drives across France to claim an inheritance, and the journey is a traffic jam of corpses, cannibals and revolutionary slogans. Jean-Luc Godard's incendiary satire is the most radical film of the New Wave — a cartoon of bourgeois greed that ends in the jungle. The eight-minute tracking shot of the traffic jam is cinema's most patient apocalypse.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the endless tracking shot along the stalled traffic — civilization at a standstill. Notice how Godard's politics are the film's structure, not its message.

name: Z (1969)
teaser: A left-wing politician is assassinated, and the investigation keeps hitting walls of official denial — until a journalist refuses to stop asking. Costa-Gavras' political thriller made the word 'Z' ('he lives') a global symbol of resistance. Filmed like a documentary, it was banned in Greece and embraced everywhere else.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the assassination is staged with newsreel immediacy. Notice how the film's suspense comes from the machinery of cover-up, not from action.

name: Pandora's Box (1929)
teaser: A beautiful, amoral woman drifts through Weimar Berlin, leaving ruined men and broken lives in her wake, until she meets her fate at the hands of Jack the Ripper. G.W. Pabst's silent classic made Louise Brooks a legend. The film's frank sensuality and its tragic final shot are the high-water mark of German cinema.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch Brooks — the camera exists to follow her. Notice how the film refuses to judge Lulu, letting the world's cruelty do the judging.

name: Freaks (1932)
teaser: A beautiful trapeze artist marries a gentle sideshow dwarf for his fortune, and the other 'freaks' — the film's true community — deliver a vengeance that horror has never matched. Tod Browning cast real sideshow performers and the studio buried the result for decades. The final scene, crawling through the mud, is unforgettable.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the wedding feast — the toast 'one of us' turns festive ritual into threat. Notice how the film's sympathies are entirely with the performers, not the 'normal' villains.

name: Trouble in Paradise (1932)
teaser: A gentleman thief and a lady pickpocket fall in love, then target the same wealthy widow — and the heist becomes a three-way seduction. Ernst Lubitsch's pre-Code comedy is the purest example of the 'Lubitsch touch': wit so light it floats. The champagne-popping opening is cinema's most elegant introduction to crime.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — a gondolier, a hotel room, and a theft conducted entirely with style. Notice how the film's morality is negotiable and its dialogue is not.

name: Duck Soup (1933)
teaser: Groucho Marx becomes the dictator of Freedonia, and the country collapses into the funniest war ever declared. The Marx Brothers' masterpiece of anarchy has no plot, no sentiment and no mercy. The mirror scene is the most famous comedy routine in film history.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the mirror routine — Harpo, Chico and Groucho improvising perfect symmetry. Notice how the film's chaos is actually choreography, timed to the frame.

name: L'Atalante (1934)
teaser: A newlywed bargeman brings his wife aboard his barge, and the cramped floating world tests their young love until a cat, a phonograph and a journey to Paris bring them back. Jean Vigo's only feature was cut and lost, then restored as one of cinema's most tender films. The underwater waltz is pure poetry.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the underwater scene — a dream of drowning and desire. Notice how the film's small world becomes a universe: the barge is all of life.

name: Bride of Frankenstein (1935)
teaser: Dr. Frankenstein is blackmailed into building a companion for his creature, and the monster — who has learned to speak, to long, to pray — finally meets a being made for him. James Whale's sequel is the rare horror film that is also a tragedy. Elsa Lanchester's hissing bride is cinema's greatest haircut and heartbreak.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the creature's encounter with the blind hermit — the film's brief moment of peace. Notice how the monster is the film's most human character.

name: The Awful Truth (1937)
teaser: A couple divorces and then spends the whole film sabotaging each other's new romances, because neither can stand the other being happy. Leo McCarey's screwball classic made Cary Grant's deadpan and Irene Dunne's mischief a perfect pair. The ending, a hat, a dog and a fire escape, is sublime nonsense.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the custody battle over the dog — a scene of pure comic logistics. Notice how the film's plot is just an excuse for the couple to keep finding each other.

name: Bringing Up Baby (1938)
teaser: A paleontologist on the eve of his wedding loses a dinosaur bone, meets a dizzy heiress and her pet leopard named Baby, and spends a night of total chaos. Howard Hawks' screwball masterpiece is Katherine Hepburn and Cary Grant at their most unhinged. The film flopped in 1938 and is now considered the funniest movie ever made.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch Grant's torn-suit descent — comedy through wardrobe destruction. Notice how the plot accelerates into pure abstraction; coherence is the enemy.

name: Only Angels Have Wings (1939)
teaser: A band of pilots flies mail over the Andes in weather that kills them one by one, and the flyers' code — no fear, no tears, no farewells — is the film's true subject. Howard Hawks' adventure is Jean Arthur, Cary Grant and the greatest barroom community ever filmed. The final landing is the code, honored.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the hangout scenes — the pilots' rituals of poker and song. Notice how Hawks films the landings and takeoffs as the group's heartbeat.

name: The Grapes of Wrath (1940)
teaser: A Dust Bowl family is driven off their land and sets out for California, where the promised work is a lie. John Ford's adaptation of Steinbeck made the Joads America's family. Henry Fonda's final speech about the 'one big soul' remains the most stirring social statement in American cinema.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the government camp sequence — the film's glimpse of decency in a cruel world. Notice how Ford films the Joads with the dignity of a monument.

name: Rebecca (1940)
teaser: A shy young woman marries a brooding widower and moves into his estate, where the memory of his first wife, Rebecca, rules every room. Alfred Hitchcock's first American film won Best Picture, and its ghost is a woman who never appears. The final confession is one of cinema's great unravelings.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch Mrs. Danvers — the film's true villain is grief wearing a housekeeper's uniform. Notice how the film never lets you see Rebecca, which is what makes her so present.

name: The Shop Around the Corner (1940)
teaser: Two Budapest shop clerks who bicker daily are secretly the anonymous pen pals who are falling in love — and neither knows the other's identity. Ernst Lubitsch's Christmas romance is the warmest film ever made about the post office. It inspired You've Got Mail, but nothing beats the original's aching sweetness.

exploreAction.targetName: The Shop Around the Corner (1940) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the final scene — the moment the pen pals recognize each other. Notice how Lubitsch films the small shop as a world, each clerk a planet.

name: How Green Was My Valley (1941)
teaser: A Welsh mining family watches the valley, the pit and their own unity decline over a generation, seen through the youngest son's memory. John Ford's Oscar-winning film is a pastoral elegy for a lost way of life. Its final shot, a family walking into the valley, is one of cinema's great goodbyes.

exploreAction.targetName: How Green Was My Valley (1941) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the boy's perspective — every event filtered through memory's golden light. Notice how the strike and the chapel give the family its dignity and its tragedy.

name: The Glass Key (1942)
teaser: A political fixer takes a beating and a bullet for his boss, a crooked mayoral candidate, and the mystery turns on loyalty's price. Stuart Heisler's pre-noir is one of the first films to map the gangster world onto politics. Alan Ladd and Veronica Lake made the film a double bill with noir's future.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the beating scene — loyalty filmed as masochism. Notice how the film's violence is psychological; the blows land offscreen.

name: Ivan the Terrible Part I (1944)
teaser: The young Ivan IV is crowned Tsar of Russia and must break the boyars' power to unite the nation — a historical epic that is really about Stalin. Sergei Eisenstein's film is opera, icon and propaganda in one. Prokofiev's score and the famous color finale make it the most majestic film ever made for a tyrant.

exploreAction.targetName: Ivan the Terrible Part I (1944) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the coronation — Eisenstein turns history into a rite. Notice how the film's grandeur is the point: power filmed as a sacred mystery.

name: The Killers (1946)
teaser: Two hitmen arrive at a diner to kill a man who is waiting for them, and an insurance investigator reconstructs the victim's life to find out why. Robert Siodmak's noir opens with the genre's most famous scene and then works backward. Burt Lancaster's debut made him a star.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the diner, the killers, and a man who chose to die. Notice how the flashbacks keep revealing the same story from new angles.

name: A Matter of Life and Death (1946)
teaser: A British pilot jumps from his burning plane without a parachute — and because of a celestial clerical error, he survives, forcing Heaven to hold a trial for his soul. Powell and Pressburger's fantasy is a Technicolor heaven versus a black-and-white afterlife courtroom. David Niven argues for love; the film is the argument.

exploreAction.targetName: A Matter of Life and Death (1946) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the transition from color to monochrome as the pilot's fate shifts. Notice how the film's trial is really about whether the heart has jurisdiction over the mind.

name: Odd Man Out (1947)
teaser: A wounded IRA man on the run from a Belfast manhunt is passed from hand to hand — each person deciding whether to help, betray or kill him. Carol Reed's film is a noir-catholic passion play about a city's conscience. James Mason's dying walk through the streets is the film's slow, luminous end.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the parade of strangers — each face a moral choice. Notice how Reed lights the night city as a place of both refuge and betrayal.

name: Black Narcissus (1947)
teaser: A convent of nuns establishes a mission in a Himalayan palace, and the thin mountain air, the wind and the memories of a former prince's pleasure garden undo their discipline. Powell and Pressburger's film is a masterpiece of atmosphere — the mountains are painted, the psychology is real. It won the Oscar for its color.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the wind — the film's antagonist, blowing through the mission like temptation. Notice how the nuns' repression is filmed with the same beauty as their release.

name: Force of Evil (1948)
teaser: A Wall Street lawyer who has laundered his numbers-racket brother's money watches the racket swallow them both. Abraham Polonsky's noir is a bare, beautiful sermon on greed, filmed against real New York streets. The final line, 'I did it for money', is the whole film in four words.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the numbers — the film treats gambling as a system, then as a fate. Notice how the brother's love and the money are the same trap.

name: The Heiress (1949)
teaser: A shy, plain heiress is courted by a charming fortune hunter, and her cruel father is certain he is a fraud — but no one is certain enough. William Wyler's adaptation of Henry James is a tragedy of trust and inheritance. Olivia de Havilland's final exit, shutting the door on love, is the most perfect revenge in American cinema.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the staircase scene — the heiress ascending with her new confidence. Notice how the film lets you hope against all evidence, then pays for that hope.

name: The Set-Up (1949)
teaser: An aging boxer refuses to throw a fight, and the men who bet against him come for him afterward. Robert Wise's film runs in almost real time — one fight, one night, one doomed act of pride. Robert Ryan's performance makes the ring a stage for dignity.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the clock — the film's real-time structure tightens every scene. Notice how the boxing is the least violent part of the night.

name: Gun Crazy (1950)
teaser: A boy who loves guns meets the woman who loves him, and together they rob banks across America until the law — and their own darkness — closes in. Joseph H. Lewis' B-movie is the most romantic and violent crime film of its era. The bank robbery filmed in one unbroken car shot is legendary.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the single-shot robbery — the camera inside the car, no cuts, pure crime. Notice how the film's lovers are doomed by the one thing they share.

name: Los Olvidados (1950)
teaser: A gang of street children in Mexico City survives on theft, violence and dreams, and the city's poverty eats them one by one. Luis Buñuel's film blends documentary cruelty with surrealist poetry — the dream sequence of a mother offering raw meat is unforgettable. It is the director's great act of social fury.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the dream sequence — Buñuel's surrealism meets the slum's real hunger. Notice how the film refuses sentiment; the children are not cute, they are casualties.

name: Orpheus (1950)
teaser: A poet is lured from his wife by Death herself, who arrives in a chauffeured Rolls-Royce, and he follows her through mirrors into the underworld. Jean Cocteau's modern retelling of the myth is surrealism at its most elegant. The reverse-played car scene and the mirror passage remain magic.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the mirrors — the film's doors to the underworld. Notice how Cocteau uses the simplest tricks to make the impossible feel inevitable.

name: The Browning Version (1951)
teaser: A hated, dry classics teacher, forced into retirement, receives a gift that exposes the boy he once was — and the man he has become. Anthony Asquith's film is a small masterpiece of humiliation and redemption. Michael Redgrave's final breakdown is one of acting's great moments.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the moment the boy gives him the book — the film's entire emotional engine. Notice how the teacher's bitterness is earned, then dismantled.

name: Othello (1952)
teaser: A general's trusted lieutenant convinces him his wife is unfaithful, and jealousy does the rest. Orson Welles' self-financed epic of shadows and voices is the greatest Shakespeare on film. The opening funeral procession, the whispered poisonings and the murder of Desdemona are filmed like a fever.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch Iago — Welles plays the villain's logic as seduction. Notice how the film's low angles and giant shadows make every scene a conspiracy.

name: Limelight (1952)
teaser: A washed-up music-hall clown saves a young ballerina from suicide and finds in her care a reason to return to the stage. Charlie Chaplin's most personal film is a meditation on age, art and the spotlight's cruelty. The final duet with Buster Keaton — the two great comedians together — is one of cinema's most moving scenes.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the final performance — Chaplin and Keaton, old masters bowing together. Notice how the film turns comedy's grace into an elegy for the stage.

name: The Band Wagon (1953)
teaser: A fading song-and-dance man teams with a pretentious director on a musical that is a flop until it becomes something else entirely. Vincente Minnelli's backstage musical is the smartest film about show business ever made. 'That's Entertainment!' and the 'Girl Hunt' ballet are the summit of the genre.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the 'Girl Hunt' ballet — a noir musical in miniature, all cigarette smoke and jazz. Notice how the film mocks pretension and then produces genuine art.

name: Ugetsu (1953)
teaser: Two peasants in war-torn 16th-century Japan chase fortune and fame — one into a ghost's palace, the other into a soldier's glory — and both pay with their families. Kenji Mizoguchi's ghost story is also a film about greed and guilt. The final shot, a mother's return, is one of cinema's great reconciliations.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the ghost's palace — a house of delusion filmed in long, gliding shots. Notice how Mizoguchi's supernatural is really the men's own vanity made visible.

name: Monsieur Hulot's Holiday (1953)
teaser: A vacationing seaside town is gently dismantled by the bumbling Monsieur Hulot, whose silent misadventures turn ordinary life into comedy. Jacques Tati's first Hulot film is a string of perfectly timed sight gags with barely a plot. Tati's baffled, pipe-smoking Everyman made him Chaplin's true heir.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the background — the jokes are everywhere, including where you aren't looking. Notice how Tati lets scenes breathe; the comedy is in the waiting.

name: The Wages of Fear (1953)
teaser: Four desperate men drive two trucks loaded with nitroglycerin over 300 miles of mountain road, and every bump is a death sentence. Henri-Georges Clouzot's thriller is the most suspenseful film ever made — Hitchcock reportedly admitted defeat. The ending's irony is the cruelest in cinema.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the oil-pool crossing — a scene of pure, unbearable tension. Notice how the film's poverty forces the men to risk death for the price of escape.

name: Hobson's Choice (1954)
teaser: A tyrannical bootmaker expects his daughters to stay home and serve him, until the eldest takes matters — and the family business — into her own hands. David Lean's comedy of domestic revolution stars Charles Laughton at his most magnificently terrible. The phrase 'Hobson's choice' — no choice at all — gets its full revenge.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch Maggie — the film's true hero, who treats her father like a problem to be solved. Notice how Lean keeps the comedy warm even as the bootmaker is dismantled.

name: The Golden Coach (1952)
teaser: An 18th-century actress in colonial Peru is courted by a viceroy, a bullfighter and a soldier — and she chooses, gloriously, the theater. Jean Renoir's film is a comedy about the art of performance, filmed in sumptuous color. The final scene, the actress choosing her empty stage, is Renoir's manifesto.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the coach — a symbol that keeps changing owners and meanings. Notice how the film's colors stage every scene like a painting by its own set designer.

name: The Killing (1956)
teaser: A career criminal assembles a team for a racetrack heist timed to the second — and every member's weakness is already scheduled to betray them. Stanley Kubrick's early noir tells the caper from each thief's point of view, out of order. The final scene, money scattered in the wind, is noir's cruelest joke.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the fractured timeline — Kubrick assembles the heist from overlapping fragments. Notice how every perfect plan is undone by the smallest human flaw.

name: The Man Who Knew Too Much (1956)
teaser: A vacationing doctor overhears a plot to assassinate a statesman in London, and the killers take his son to guarantee his silence. Hitchcock's remake of his own 1934 film builds to the Albert Hall concert, where the assassin's cue is a clash of cymbals. Doris Day's 'Que Sera, Sera' becomes a weapon.

exploreAction.targetName: The Man Who Knew Too Much (1956) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the concert sequence — twenty minutes of pure suspense built on a cymbal. Notice how Hitchcock withholds every release until the audience is begging.

name: Written on the Wind (1956)
teaser: A Texas oil dynasty's heirs — an alcoholic playboy and his sister — destroy themselves with jealousy, and the one sane man in the house is framed for their sins. Douglas Sirk's melodrama is a mirror held to America's postwar glamour. The film's colors, shadows and hysteria made it the art-house favorite it was never meant to be.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the color — Sirk's palette is the film's unconscious, screaming what the dialogue won't say. Notice how the characters' wealth is a cage, not a prize.

name: The Sweet Smell of Success (1957)
teaser: A powerful gossip columnist and a desperate press agent trade favors, lies and souls in the city's night, each believing he controls the other. Alexander Mackendrick's film is the most cynical ever made about New York power. Tony Curtis and Burt Lancaster's venomous duet is the definitive portrait of ambition without limits.

exploreAction.targetName: The Sweet Smell of Success (1957) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the dialogue — every line is a knife, and the film is the duel. Notice how the jazz score and the neon make the city the third villain.

name: A Man Escaped (1956)
teaser: A captured Resistance fighter plans an escape from a Nazi prison cell, using a spoon, a rope of scraps and total patience. Robert Bresson's film is a spiritual exercise disguised as a thriller — every detail is the plot. The final cut of the rope is one of cinema's great releases of held breath.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the sounds — footsteps, keys, scraping metal; the film is built on what is heard. Notice how Bresson's restraint makes the escape an act of faith.

name: The Guns of Navarone (1961)
teaser: A team of commandos must destroy two German cannons that command a vital sea passage — and the mission's biggest enemy is time. J. Lee Thompson's war epic is the template for the mission film, with Gregory Peck, David Niven and Anthony Quinn. The cliff-climb and the final gun duel are pure adventure cinema.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the infiltration — the film's suspense is procedural, each plan unravelling. Notice how the team's rivalries are as dangerous as the enemy.

name: Ball of Fire (1941)
teaser: A team of dictionary scholars, led by the stiffest professor alive, discovers that their newest source on slang is a nightclub singer hiding from gangsters. Howard Hawks balances farce and romance perfectly, with Gary Cooper learning the word 'yum-yum' and Barbara Stanwyck teaching a whole academy about the modern world.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the seven professors become a comedy chorus. Notice that every new slang word they learn signals a step deeper into danger and desire.

name: Gilda (1946)
teaser: A gambler takes a job at a Buenos Aires casino owned by a ruthless man, only to find the boss's wife is the woman he once loved. Glenn Ford burns with jealousy and Rita Hayworth delivers the most famous hair flip in cinema history. A noir built entirely on looks, sneers, and the threat of violence under silk.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch Hayworth's first entrance and the 'Put the Blame on Mame' number. Notice how the camera treats Gilda as an object the men fight over — until she starts fighting back.

name: A Letter to Three Wives (1949)
teaser: Three women on a river outing each receive a letter from the town's most magnetic woman, saying she has run off with one of their husbands — but not which one. Joseph L. Mankiewicz structures the film as three flashbacks of doubt and memory. It won him the first of consecutive Best Director Oscars.

exploreAction.targetName: A Letter to Three Wives (1949) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how each flashback reveals what the wife fears and what she knows. Notice that the letter is never opened at the end — the uncertainty is the point.

name: The Bad and the Beautiful (1952)
teaser: A ruthless producer who cheated, used, and discarded the people who made him famous tries to lure them back for one last picture. Three flashbacks show him through the eyes of a director, a writer, and an actress. Kirk Douglas makes the monster magnetic. It won five Oscars, including Best Supporting Actress.

exploreAction.targetName: The Bad and the Beautiful (1952) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch each flashback shift the story's sympathy. Notice how Minnelli frames Hollywood glamour as a machine that eats its own people.

name: From Here to Eternity (1953)
teaser: On a Hawaiian Army base on the eve of Pearl Harbor, a defiant private who can box refuses to join the boxing team, and a captain's wife falls for a sergeant. The beach kiss with waves crashing over Burt Lancaster and Deborah Kerr is cinema's most famous embrace. Eight Oscars followed.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the famous beach scene in context — it is a single minute of stolen happiness in a film full of rigid discipline. Notice how the attack changes every character's story.

name: Shane (1953)
teaser: A quiet gunslinger rides into a Wyoming valley and is drawn into a war between homesteaders and a cattle baron. A boy narrates the story, and the film is told through his worshipful eyes. Alan Ladd's Shane is the archetype of the lone gunman who saves the family and rides away.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch Shane's two costume changes — from buckskin to black and back. Notice how the boy's point of view turns a Western into a myth about growing up.

name: The Seven Year Itch (1955)
teaser: A married man's wife leaves for the summer, and his fantasies about the woman upstairs — the blonde with the white dress and the subway grate — run wild. Billy Wilder's adaptation of his own play gave Marilyn Monroe her signature image. It is a comedy about what happens in a man's head when nobody is watching.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the split between Tom's real life and his fantasy narrator. Notice how the film's censors-forced restraint actually makes the longing funnier.

name: Witness for the Prosecution (1957)
teaser: A barrister defending a man accused of murder faces the impossible: the only witness for the prosecution is the defendant's own wife, and she is testifying against him. Billy Wilder's courtroom drama, from an Agatha Christie play, saves its twist for the very last line. Charles Laughton is magnificent as the ailing, wry counsel.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the final scene carefully — Wilder asks you to keep a secret. Notice how the 'impossible' evidence was planted in plain sight.

name: The Defiant Ones (1958)
teaser: Two escaped convicts — one Black, one white — are chained together and must cooperate or die in the Louisiana swamp. Stanley Kramer's message picture pairs Sidney Poitier and Tony Curtis, who both earned Oscar nominations. The chain is the film's whole metaphor, worn with increasing weight as the men learn each other.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the chain changes from a physical link into a moral one. Notice the famous mud-pit rescue — the moment the metaphor becomes literal.

name: The Magnificent Seven (1960)
teaser: A Mexican village, terrorized by bandits, pools its pennies to hire seven gunmen to defend it. John Sturges remade Kurosawa's Seven Samurai as a Western, with a cast including Yul Brynner, Steve McQueen, and Charles Bronson. Elmer Bernstein's galloping theme became one of the most recognizable scores ever written.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how each of the seven is introduced as a distinct character. Notice the theme music doing the storytelling between scenes — it carries the whole mood.

name: Judgment at Nuremberg (1961)
teaser: Four German judges who served under the Nazis face trial for crimes committed in the name of law. Spencer Tracy presides over a courtroom where the question is not guilt but civilization itself. Stanley Kramer's film assembles an all-star cast and asks whether obeying orders can excuse the worst of crimes.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the testimony of the woman sterilized by a court order — the film's most devastating scene. Notice how each verdict reopens the argument about responsibility.

name: Lolita (1962)
teaser: A middle-aged professor becomes obsessed with his landlady's fourteen-year-old daughter and marries the mother to stay close. Stanley Kubrick's adaptation of Nabokov's scandalous novel turns censorship into a strange strength, keeping the desire in words and glances. James Mason and Sue Lyon make the unthinkable watchable.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening scene, which starts at the end. Notice how Kubrick stages the forbidden relationship as a comedy of manners gone horribly wrong.

name: The Days of Wine and Roses (1962)
teaser: A public relations man and the pretty secretary he marries discover that together they make a perfect drinking team. Jack Lemmon and Lee Remick chart the course from social drinking to full collapse in Blake Edwards's uncompromising drama. The candy-bar craving scene is a landmark of raw acting.

exploreAction.targetName: The Days of Wine and Roses (1962) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the greenhouse scene where Joe refuses to let Kirsten sober up alone. Notice how Edwards never glamorizes the drinking — every party ends in wreckage.

name: Charade (1963)
teaser: A woman returns from a ski trip to find her husband murdered, and every man she turns to — including Cary Grant's charming stranger — seems to want the fortune he left behind. Audrey Hepburn and Grant glide through a thriller that never stops being a comedy. The script is full of double crosses that keep paying off.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening credits, where the bodies fall before the film even starts. Notice how Grant plays every scene like he might be the villain.

name: The Producers (1967)
teaser: A washed-up Broadway producer and his nervous accountant decide to oversell shares in a guaranteed flop and keep the money when it closes. Mel Brooks's directorial debut, starring Zero Mostel and Gene Wilder, gambles on a musical called Springtime for Hitler. It won Brooks the Oscar for Best Original Screenplay.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the 'Springtime for Hitler' number — a full-scale Nazi musical staged with tap-dancing storm troopers. Notice how Brooks makes bad taste a tool of comedy.

name: The Lion in Winter (1968)
teaser: King Henry II assembles his wife Eleanor and their squabbling sons for a Christmas court where the succession of England is decided by wit, threats, and betrayal. Peter O'Toole and Katharine Hepburn match each other line for line in a family argument that doubles as a history lesson. Hepburn won her third Oscar here.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the chess match of alliances that shifts every ten minutes. Notice how the film never leaves the castle — the entire war is fought in one room.

name: Bullitt (1968)
teaser: A San Francisco detective protecting a mob witness watches him get murdered anyway, and sets out to find out why. Steve McQueen's cool minimalism made Bullitt the template for the modern action hero. The car chase down the city's hills — real cars, real speed, no music — is the most famous chase ever filmed.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the chase: no score, no dialogue, just engines. Notice how McQueen does more acting by saying less than almost any other leading man.

name: Easy Rider (1969)
teaser: Two bikers ride their choppers from Los Angeles to New Orleans with drug money sewn into the gas tank, looking for America. Dennis Hopper's counterculture landmark, starring Peter Fonda and Jack Nicholson, captured a generation's unease with the establishment. The soundtrack — Steppenwolf, the Byrds, Hendrix — became a playlist for the era.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film as a road trip through a country that does not want its riders. Notice how the acid-tripping cemetery scene turns the American dream into a vision of death.

name: Love Story (1970)
teaser: A wealthy preppy and a working-class music student meet at Harvard, fall in love, and defy their families until tragedy intervenes. Arthur Hiller's romance made 'Love means never having to say you're sorry' one of the most quoted — and parodied — lines in cinema. Ryan O'Neal and Ali MacGraw became the decade's most iconic couple.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the ice-skating scenes and the famous line in context. Notice how the film made a generation cry while critics called it sentimental — both are true.

name: Klute (1971)
teaser: A small-town detective comes to New York to find a missing executive, and his only lead is a high-priced call girl who knew the man. Jane Fonda's Oscar-winning performance as Bree Daniel, all guarded intelligence and frayed nerves, elevated a detective story into a character study. Alan J. Pakula directs the first of his paranoia trilogy.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch Fonda's audition-as-confession scene, where Bree performs herself. Notice how Pakula shoots the city as a maze that watches its women.

name: Fiddler on the Roof (1971)
teaser: A milkman in a Jewish shtetl in 1905 Russia tries to hold his family and traditions together as his daughters marry against custom and the village itself begins to scatter. Topol's Tevye anchors Norman Jewison's lavish adaptation of the Broadway musical. 'Tradition!' opens it; a train of exiles closes it.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the 'Sunrise, Sunset' wedding and the dream sequence with the ghost. Notice how the songs carry the history — each tradition questioned is a world disappearing.

name: Deliverance (1972)
teaser: Four city men take a canoe trip down a Georgia river that is about to be dammed, and the wilderness turns savage. John Boorman's survival thriller contains the most disturbing scene in 1970s cinema, plus the haunting 'dueling banjos' duet. Jon Voight, Burt Reynolds, and Ned Beatty went from tourists to survivors.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the banjo duel — the film's most famous moment and its least violent. Notice how the river itself becomes an enemy the men must escape twice.

name: Sounder (1972)
teaser: In Depression-era Louisiana, a Black sharecropper is sentenced to hard labor for stealing food, and his family must survive a year without him. Cicely Tyson's quiet strength and Paul Winfield's dignity made this one of the first major studio films to center a Black family's ordinary life. The father-son scenes cut deep.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the trial scene, where the family's whole future is decided in minutes. Notice how the film refuses melodrama — the hardship is in the waiting.

name: American Graffiti (1973)
teaser: One summer night in 1962, a group of California teenagers cruise the strip, race cars, and say goodbye to each other before college takes them apart. George Lucas's love letter to his own youth launched Richard Dreyfuss, Harrison Ford, and the nostalgia industry. Wolfman Jack provides the soundtrack from beyond the radio.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film as a clock — the night is measured in songs and near-misses. Notice how Lucas sets four storylines in motion and weaves them through the same streets.

name: Paper Moon (1973)
teaser: A con man traveling Depression-era Kansas takes along a nine-year-old girl who may be his daughter — and who turns out to be a sharper grifter than he is. Ryan O'Neal and his real daughter Tatum O'Neal, the youngest Oscar winner ever, make the grift a family affair. The final shot is one of the great ambiguous endings.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how Addie's sales pitch improves every time Moses blunders. Notice the final freeze-frame — the con continues, or it doesn't, and both readings work.

name: Serpico (1973)
teaser: A young New York cop refuses the payoff money every other cop takes, and his honesty turns him into a pariah on the force. Al Pacino's shaggy, furious performance made Frank Serpico a symbol of the lone whistleblower. Sidney Lumet shot the city's streets like a war zone of blue uniforms.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch Pacino's growing isolation — every scene with other cops is a scene of pressure. Notice how the film builds to the famous shooting and the trial that followed.

name: The Texas Chain Saw Massacre (1974)
teaser: Five friends on a road trip stop at an abandoned farmhouse and meet the cannibalistic Sawyer family, including Leatherface and his roaring chainsaw. Tobe Hooper's grindhouse shocker was made for under 300,000 dollars and terrified audiences for decades. Its power lies in suggestion — the worst horrors are implied, not shown.

exploreAction.targetName: The Texas Chain Saw Massacre (1974) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how Hooper uses the Texas heat and the sound design to build dread. Notice the dinner table scene — the film's centerpiece of horror staged like a family meal.

name: Coming Home (1978)
teaser: A Marine captain's wife volunteers at a VA hospital while her husband serves in Vietnam and falls in love with a paralyzed veteran who has come home bitter and angry. Hal Ashby's drama, starring Jane Fonda and Jon Voight, gave both actors Oscars. The film asked what 'coming home' meant for a country at war with itself.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the famous supermarket scene, where the wheelchair forces the world to look. Notice how the music — including a Jimi Hendrix cover — carries the era.

name: Superman (1978)
teaser: The last son of Krypton lands on Earth, grows up in Smallville, and moves to Metropolis, where he fights crime as Clark Kent by day and saves the world as Superman by night. Christopher Reeve made the role definitive with a single costume change. The John Williams theme is instantly recognizable anywhere on Earth.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the 'You've got me? Who's got you?' moment and the helicopter rescue. Notice how Reeve plays Clark and Superman as two entirely different people.

name: All That Jazz (1979)
teaser: A choreographer who works himself to death, chain-smoking, womanizing, and directing a Broadway show while his heart fails, imagines his own death as a musical number. Bob Fosse's brutally honest self-portrait stars Roy Scheider as his stand-in. The final 'Bye Bye Life' number is one of cinema's greatest finales.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the constant cutting between the show and the hospital. Notice how the film makes death a performer — the Angel of Death dances with him through his last act.

name: Ordinary People (1980)
teaser: A family that looks perfect from the outside — a lawyer father, a precise mother, a surviving son — collapses after the older son drowns. Robert Redford's directorial debut, starring Donald Sutherland, Mary Tyler Moore, and a young Timothy Hutton, is a study of grief that cannot be spoken. Hutton won Best Supporting Actor.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the therapy sessions, where the movie's real action happens. Notice how Moore's perfection is the tragedy — she is as frozen as the son who drowned.

name: Reds (1981)
teaser: An idealistic American journalist and his free-spirited lover travel to Russia to cover the Bolshevik revolution and watch their romance and their politics collide with history. Warren Beatty's sweeping epic about John Reed and Louise Bryant won him the Best Director Oscar. Real witnesses to the era are interviewed between scenes.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the 'witness' interviews — real veterans of the era speak directly to camera. Notice how the personal and political storylines mirror each other's rise and fall.

name: Body Heat (1981)
teaser: A small-town Florida lawyer meets a wealthy man's wife on a sweltering night, and the affair turns into a plot to kill her husband. Lawrence Kasdan's directorial debut, starring William Hurt and Kathleen Turner, revived the film noir with sweaty, explicit heat. Turner's first film made her an instant femme fatale icon.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the heat is a character — every window is open, every shirt is wet. Notice how Kasdan withholds the twist until the very last scene on the beach.

name: Gandhi (1982)
teaser: A shy lawyer in South Africa discovers the power of nonviolent resistance and spends fifty years leading India's independence movement without firing a shot. Richard Attenborough's epic, starring Ben Kingsley in an Oscar-winning performance, spans decades and continents. The funeral pyre scene became an icon of world cinema.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the salt march — a protest built on walking and patience. Notice how Kingsley disappears into the role so completely that he stops resembling an actor.

name: Trading Places (1983)
teaser: Two wealthy brothers make a bet that they can turn a street hustler into a respectable trader while reducing their own pampered protégé to crime. Eddie Murphy and Dan Aykroyd trade places in a satire of class and luck. The film's ending, a commodities-market heist, is one of the great comic climaxes.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the bet being made in the opening scene — it sets up everything. Notice how the film uses real economics: the orange juice futures finale is a genuine market play.

name: Beverly Hills Cop (1984)
teaser: A Detroit detective with an attitude follows his best friend's murder trail to Beverly Hills, where the local police want him gone. Eddie Murphy's fast-talking Axel Foley became the defining action-comedy role of the Eighties. The film's needle-drop of 'Axel F' by Harold Faltermeyer is iconic.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch Foley improvise his way past every obstacle with lies and nerve. Notice how Murphy's comedy carries the action — the shootouts are excuses for his wit.

name: Out of Africa (1985)
teaser: A Danish baroness runs a coffee plantation in colonial Kenya and falls into a fierce, impossible love with a big-game hunter. Meryl Streep and Robert Redford play the affair against the backdrop of the African highlands, shot like a painting. The film won seven Oscars, including Best Picture and Best Director.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the aerial shots over the savanna — the landscape is the film's third character. Notice how the affair is told through memory, from the moment it is already over.

name: Hannah and Her Sisters (1986)
teaser: Three sisters in Manhattan orbit each other over two Thanksgivings, and every one of them is secretly rearranging her life. Woody Allen's ensemble comedy-drama follows a hypochondriac, an actress, and a woman married to a man who loves her sister. It won three Oscars, including Best Supporting Actor for Michael Caine.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the structure — the story circles the same holiday table twice. Notice how Allen moves between characters, letting every secret surface and settle.

name: The Untouchables (1987)
teaser: A treasury agent assembles a squad of honest cops to bring down Al Capone, who owns the city and the courts. Sean Connery's beat cop won an Oscar for the film's most famous line — 'Here endeth the lesson.' Brian De Palma stages a shootout on the steps of Union Station that rivals the Odessa Steps.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the baby carriage rolling down the steps during the shootout — a deliberate homage. Notice how De Palma turns the historical case into pure opera.

name: Broadcast News (1987)
teaser: A smart, anxious producer, a principled anchor, and a handsome empty suit compete for the future of television news, and the fight gets personal. James L. Brooks's smart romantic comedy-drama stars Holly Hunter, William Hurt, and Albert Brooks. The famous breakdown scene — a single tear — is a masterclass.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the scene where Jane can't stop crying on air. Notice how the film asks whether honesty and charisma can ever share the same newscast.

name: The Last Emperor (1987)
teaser: Puyi, the last emperor of China, is crowned at age three and lives through palace luxury, revolution, prison, and finally a job as a gardener. Bernardo Bertolucci's epic was the first Western film allowed to shoot inside the Forbidden City. It won all nine Oscars it was nominated for.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the flashback structure — every scene in prison echoes a scene in the palace. Notice how the film uses color to separate the emperor's two lives.

name: Big (1988)
teaser: A twelve-year-old boy wishes to be big, wakes up in an adult's body, and gets a job at a toy company where his child's-eye view is a business genius. Tom Hanks made his stardom debut with the piano-store duet and the famous 'I don't get it' line. The film asks what adults lose when they grow up.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the F.A.O. Schwarz scene, where Josh plays 'Heart and Soul' on the giant keyboard. Notice how Hanks plays every scene as a boy trapped in a man's body.

name: Coming to America (1988)
teaser: The crown prince of the fictional African nation of Zamunda travels to Queens, New York, to find a bride who loves him for himself, not his title. Eddie Murphy and Arsenio Hall play a dozen characters under heavy makeup. The barbershop scenes became comedy history.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the barbershop regulars — Murphy and Hall under layers of prosthetics. Notice how the film satirizes both royal excess and American striving with the same grin.

name: Field of Dreams (1989)
teaser: An Iowa farmer hears a voice telling him to build a baseball diamond in his cornfield, and the ghosts of past players come to play. Kevin Costner's magical fable about fathers and forgiveness became an instant classic. The line 'If you build it, he will come' entered the language.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the final scene between Ray and his father — the film's whole point arrives as a catch. Notice how the movie never explains the magic; it just lets it happen.

name: sex, lies, and videotape (1989)
teaser: A drifting stranger arrives in Baton Rouge and asks everyone he meets to confess their secrets on video, upending a marriage, a career, and a friendship. Steven Soderbergh made this debut for 1.2 million dollars, and it won the Palme d'Or. The film announced the independent cinema boom of the Nineties.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the video confessions shift power from the talkers to the listener. Notice how Soderbergh's quiet style lets the performances carry everything.

name: Driving Miss Daisy (1989)
teaser: An aging Jewish widow in Atlanta and her proud Black chauffeur form a friendship that spans twenty-five years of American change. Jessica Tandy became the oldest Best Actress winner ever, and Morgan Freeman's Hoke is a portrait of quiet dignity. The film won Best Picture at the Oscars.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the small gestures — the biscuit, the picnic, the hand on the arm. Notice how the decades pass in news headlines, while the friendship just keeps driving.

name: Ghost (1990)
teaser: A murdered banker refuses to leave this world, and with the help of a fake psychic he tries to warn the girlfriend who still loves him. Patrick Swayze, Demi Moore, and Whoopi Goldberg, who won an Oscar, made the pottery-wheel scene the most romantic image of the decade. The film mixes the supernatural, comedy, and grief.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the 'Unchained Melody' pottery scene — quiet, sensual, and later devastating. Notice how the film earns its comedy and its tears in equal measure.

name: Boyz n the Hood (1991)
teaser: Three friends grow up in South Central Los Angeles, where graduation, fatherhood, and survival are all uncertain. John Singleton became the youngest director ever nominated for an Oscar with this debut. The film's warning — 'Any fool with a dick can make a baby' — still lands like a punch.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the graduation-then-gunfire ending and the two paths the same night takes. Notice how Singleton balances the neighborhood's joy and its danger in the same frame.

name: The Fugitive (1993)
teaser: A Chicago surgeon convicted of murdering his wife escapes from a wrecked prison bus and hunts for the one-armed man while a relentless federal marshal hunts for him. Harrison Ford runs and Tommy Lee Jones, in an Oscar-winning turn, chases with deadpan genius. The dam scene is one of cinema's great stunts.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the hospital escape, where the hunter and hunted are feet apart. Notice how the film never cheats the chase — every move is earned and every step is logic.

name: Leaving Las Vegas (1995)
teaser: A screenwriter who has decided to drink himself to death and a prostitute who has decided she will not fall in love meet in Las Vegas and keep each other's promises. Nicolas Cage won the Oscar for the film's suicide as seduction. Mike Figgis shot it fast and cheap, and the honesty shows.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how Ben's drinking is treated without judgment — it is simply his plan. Notice how the film never moralizes, which is exactly why it devastates.

name: Shakespeare in Love (1998)
teaser: A struggling young playwright with writer's block falls for a noblewoman who wants to act, and the affair becomes Romeo and Juliet. Tom Stoppard's Oscar-winning script turns Shakespeare's biography into a backstage romance. Gwyneth Paltrow, Judi Dench, and a surprise cameo make it a love letter to theater.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the play and the love affair interleave — the balcony scene is rehearsed as real courtship. Notice the ending, where the lovers part so the art can live.

name: Magnolia (1999)
teaser: One rainy San Fernando Valley day, nine lives collide — a dying father, a lost son, a strung-out former child star, a police officer in love, and a quiz-show prodigy. Paul Thomas Anderson's ensemble epic builds to the most bizarre rainstorm ever filmed. Tom Cruise's Oscar-nominated 'respect the cock' performance is unforgettable.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening montage of coincidences — the film is about how chance stacks up. Notice how every character's song, 'Wise Up,' arrives in a single synchronized shot.

name: Traffic (2000)
teaser: A conservative judge becomes the drug czar just as his own daughter sinks into addiction, while a cop on the border and a DEA agent chase a cartel. Steven Soderbergh's ensemble drama tells three stories in three color palettes and won four Oscars. The film refuses easy villains.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how each storyline has its own color and grain — Mexico sepia, Washington blue, San Diego overexposed. Notice how the war on drugs is shown from every side at once.

name: Capote (2005)
teaser: Truman Capote spends six years in Kansas researching the murder of a farm family, and the book that makes his career also destroys him. Philip Seymour Hoffman's Oscar-winning performance captures the writer's fascination and guilt. Bennett Miller's debut is a study of the price of great art.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the prison interviews, where Capote and Perry become mirror images. Notice how the film never shows Capote writing — it shows him feeding on the story.

name: Walk the Line (2005)
teaser: Johnny Cash rises from an Arkansas cotton farm to music stardom, fighting pills, prison, and his own demons, with June Carter the only woman who can save him. Joaquin Phoenix and Reese Witherspoon did their own singing in James Mangold's biography. Witherspoon won the Oscar for Best Actress.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the Folsom Prison concert — the moment Cash finally turns his pain into performance. Notice how the songs are not covers but scenes: each one tells his story.

name: The Diving Bell and the Butterfly (2007)
teaser: The editor of French Elle suffers a massive stroke and is left with 'locked-in syndrome' — fully conscious but able to move only his left eyelid. Julian Schnabel's film tells Jean-Dominique Bauby's story from inside his own head, with the camera as his blinking eye. He dictated his memoir one blink at a time.

exploreAction.targetName: The Diving Bell and the Butterfly (2007) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening, shot entirely from Bauby's point of view as the doctors loom over him. Notice how the film's perspective gradually widens as his inner life expands.

name: Juno (2007)
teaser: A sixteen-year-old with a deadpan wit finds herself pregnant and decides to give the baby to a seemingly perfect couple, only to discover nobody is perfect. Ellen Page's Juno, written by Diablo Cody, turned a teen pregnancy into a funny, warm, honest comedy. It earned four Oscar nominations, winning Best Original Screenplay.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch Juno's armor — the sarcasm is her way of staying in control. Notice how the film treats every character with generosity, even the ones who fail.

name: Milk (2008)
teaser: Harvey Milk, the first openly gay man elected to major public office in the United States, built a movement in San Francisco before being assassinated in 1978. Sean Penn's Oscar-winning performance turns history into a portrait of courage and hope. Gus Van Sant's film ends with candles and the speech Milk recorded in case of his death.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the recorded 'in case of assassination' speech — the film plays it as Milk's farewell. Notice how the campaign scenes show politics as a contact sport of hope.

name: The Hurt Locker (2008)
teaser: The best bomb-disposal technician in Iraq is also the most reckless, and his new squad watches him flirt with death one wire at a time. Kathryn Bigelow became the first woman to win the Best Director Oscar with this visceral war film. The handheld cameras put you inside the bomb suit.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the bomb-disposal scenes — the tension is built entirely through sound and detail. Notice how the film refuses to judge the addiction at its center.

name: The Blind Side (2009)
teaser: A wealthy Tennessee family takes in a homeless teenager who turns out to be one of the most gifted football prospects in the country. Sandra Bullock's Oscar-winning performance as Leigh Anne Tuohy anchored this true-story crowd-pleaser. Michael Oher went on to play nine seasons in the NFL.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the film turns a sports story into a family story — the football matters less than the couch. Notice the game-tape scenes that explain Michael's instincts.

name: The Descendants (2011)
teaser: A Hawaiian lawyer with a comatose wife discovers she was having an affair, and with his two difficult daughters he goes looking for the man. George Clooney's middle-aged meltdown is one of his best performances. Alexander Payne balances grief and comedy in a land of perpetual sunshine.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch Matt's awkward anger — Clooney plays a man who never learned how to feel. Notice how Hawaii is both the setting and the irony: paradise and pain in the same frame.

name: Avatar (2009)
teaser: A paralyzed Marine is sent to the moon Pandora to infiltrate the alien Na'vi, but falls in love with the world he was sent to conquer. James Cameron's effects revolution made 3D a cultural event and became the highest-grossing film ever at the time. The bioluminescent forests remain a vision no one has topped.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the world-building — Pandora feels fully lived-in. Notice how Cameron uses the Na'vi to ask what we owe to a world we are destroying.

name: Maestro (2023)
teaser: Leonard Bernstein conducts, composes, loves, and drifts through decades of American music, with his marriage to Felicia Montealegre at the center. Bradley Cooper directs and stars, learning to conduct for real, and Carey Mulligan matches him note for note. The film's centerpiece is the Ely Cathedral conducting sequence.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the cathedral performance — a single unbroken take of Bernstein at full power. Notice how the film treats music as the language the marriage actually speaks.

name: Emilia Pérez (2024)
teaser: A feared cartel boss hires a lawyer to orchestrate his own disappearance and gender transition, then returns to reclaim his family as a woman. Jacques Audiard's genre-bending musical won the Cannes Jury Prize and eleven Oscar nominations, a record for a non-English film. Zoe Saldaña and Karla Sofía Gascón lead the cast.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the film switches registers — cartel thriller, musical, melodrama — without ever losing its center. Notice how the songs carry the emotional beats the dialogue leaves out.

name: Napoléon (1927)
teaser: Abel Gance's six-hour epic follows Napoleon from a snowball fight at military school to the Italian campaign, filmed with techniques nobody had tried before — three-screen triptychs, rapid cutting, and cameras strapped to horses. The film was restored decades later in a legendary 5-hour version. It remains the summit of silent spectacle.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the final triptych — three screens playing at once, an invention decades ahead of its time. Notice how Gance's editing moves faster than any film of its era.

name: The Crowd (1928)
teaser: An ordinary man believes he is destined for greatness, and the city slowly teaches him he is one of millions. King Vidor's silent epic follows one clerk from birth to death through marriage, layoffs, and the death of a child. Its unglamorous realism was decades ahead of its time.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening crane shot into the skyscraper windows — the individual vanishing into the mass. Notice how the film's honest ending was too bleak for its own era.

name: Tabu (1931)
teaser: A young South Seas couple defies the taboo placed on the girl's chastity and flees their island, only to find paradise cannot be escaped. F. W. Murnau's final film, made with documentarian Robert Flaherty, is a poetic tragedy shot on real locations with non-actors. Murnau died in a car crash days before its premiere.
