exploreAction.instruction: Watch the white-painted ship's arrival — the outside world invading paradise. Notice how the film was shot with real islanders and real light, a documentary wrapped in a myth.

name: The Baker's Wife (1938)
teaser: A Provençal baker's much-younger wife runs off with a handsome shepherd, and the heartbroken baker refuses to bake until she returns, holding the whole village hostage. Marcel Pagnol's comedy stars Raimu in one of cinema's great comic performances. The villagers' mission to reunite the couple is a small masterpiece of warmth.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the village debate over the baker's honor becomes a town project. Notice how the film finds both the comedy and the ache in a cuckolded man's pride.

name: Mildred Pierce (1945)
teaser: A housewife claws her way from pie-making to restaurant empire to give her cold, ambitious daughter everything — and the daughter takes everything, including the man. Joan Crawford won her only Oscar as Mildred in Michael Curtiz's noir-stained melodrama. The murder at the start is solved through flashbacks that are really a mother's confession.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the murder scene that opens the film and the flashback that explains it. Notice how the film turns a mother's sacrifice into a crime story.

name: Leave Her to Heaven (1945)
teaser: A novelist marries a beautiful woman whose love is absolute — possessive enough to drown her own unborn child rather than share her husband. Gene Tierney's Ellen is the most chilling femme fatale of classic Hollywood. The Technicolor landscapes only make the jealousy colder.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the lake scene — a swimming accident that is really a murder by omission. Notice how the film's gorgeous color makes Ellen's obsession feel like a fever dream.

name: Brief Encounter (1945)
teaser: A married suburban housewife and a married doctor meet by chance in a railway station tea room, and the affair that never quite happens changes both their lives. David Lean's adaptation of Noël Coward's play is told entirely in the woman's memory. The steam on the platform and Rachmaninoff's concerto made it the definitive forbidden-love film.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the framing — the whole story is a memory that begins with the ending. Notice how the mundane station becomes a stage for an impossible romance.

name: Duel in the Sun (1946)
teaser: A tempestuous half-breed girl raised on a Texas ranch falls for the wild son of the family while his noble brother offers her respect. King Vidor's Technicolor western, starring Jennifer Jones and Gregory Peck, was a scandal in its day for its frankness. The final duel on the rocks is one of the great operatic endings.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film's shameless melodrama — it was marketed as 'lust in the dust.' Notice how the mountain chase finale turns a western into a lovers' suicide pact.

name: My Darling Clementine (1946)
teaser: Wyatt Earp rides into Tombstone, and the gunfight at the O.K. Corral is staged as a formal, near-ritual climax. John Ford's western, starring Henry Fonda, is less about history than about the myth of the frontier — church bells, a dance floor, and a town being built. Clementine never existed as Ford tells her, and it does not matter.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the dance at the church-raising — the film's emotional center. Notice how Ford frames Monument Valley as a character that dwarfs every human story.

name: Great Expectations (1946)
teaser: A poor orphan boy meets an escaped convict in a graveyard, and that chance encounter steers his whole life toward a mysterious fortune. David Lean's adaptation of Dickens is the definitive version, with the fog, the marshes, and Miss Havisham's wedding-cake decay. It won two Oscars for its art direction and cinematography.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening graveyard scene — the fog and the terror set the tone for everything. Notice how the film treats the fortune as a trap, not a gift.

name: The Bishop's Wife (1947)
teaser: A harried bishop prays for help building a cathedral and gets an angel named Dudley, who charms his wife, his daughter, and the whole congregation — and makes the bishop wonder if he is losing his place. Cary Grant's angel is the definition of effortless charm. The film was nominated for five Oscars.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the skating scene and the snow — Grant glides through the film like the answer to every prayer. Notice how the angel's gift is not a cathedral but time for the family.

name: Oliver Twist (1948)
teaser: An orphan boy born in a workhouse runs away to London and falls in with a gang of child thieves led by the sly Fagin. David Lean's Dickens adaptation is one of the darkest films ever made for mainstream audiences, with Alec Guinness unrecognizable as Fagin. The film was banned in some cities for decades over its portrayal.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening in the workhouse — the gruel scene is cinema's most famous hunger strike. Notice how Lean turns Victorian London into a fog-drenched nightmare.

name: Rope (1948)
teaser: Two brilliant young men strangle a classmate and then host a dinner party with the body hidden in a trunk, serving the guests food from its lid. Alfred Hitchcock shot the film in long, continuous takes that appear to be one single shot. The experiment was a box-office failure and a technical landmark.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the 'one take' approach tightens the room like a drum. Notice how the hidden body and the clever host create a suspense that never lets go.

name: The Bicycle Thief (1948)
teaser: A Roman bill-poster's bicycle — his only means of work — is stolen on his first day, and he and his son spend a desperate day searching the city. Vittorio De Sica's neorealist masterpiece was made with non-professional actors and real streets. It is consistently ranked among the greatest films ever made.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the father-son relationship — the boy learns how the world works in one day. Notice how the film uses poverty as both setting and engine, with no escape hatch.

name: The Lavender Hill Mob (1951)
teaser: A timid bank clerk who has spent his career transporting gold bullion dreams of stealing it, and with an eccentric inventor he pulls off the perfect heist. Alec Guinness's comic masterwork, from Ealing Studios, is one of the great British comedies. The chase over the rooftops of London is pure joy.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the heist planning scenes — the film's real comedy is in the details. Notice how Guinness plays a man who wants to be a criminal the way other men want to retire.

name: The Bad Seed (1956)
teaser: A picture-perfect little girl with perfect manners turns out to be a cold-blooded killer, and her mother slowly realizes the truth she cannot face. Mervyn LeRoy's adaptation of the Broadway hit made Patty McCormack a child-star sensation. The film's shocking finale was softened for audiences of the day.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how Rhoda's sweetness is weaponized — every 'please' and 'thank you' hides a calculation. Notice how the stagebound setting keeps the horror intimate and psychological.

name: Steve Jobs (2015)
teaser: Three product launches — 1984, 1988, 1998 — unfold backstage as Jobs battles the people who made him: his partner, his mentor, and the daughter he refuses to acknowledge. Aaron Sorkin's screenplay gives Michael Fassbender a machine-gun role. The film is less biography than a debate about what genius costs.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the backstage structure — each launch is one continuous argument. Notice how Sorkin's dialogue turns every conversation into a chess match about truth and loyalty.

name: Carol (2015)
teaser: In 1950s New York, a young department-store clerk falls for a glamorous older woman trapped in a failing marriage, and their affair runs straight into the era's laws and social walls. Cate Blanchett and Rooney Mara give two of the decade's great performances. Todd Haynes films their love in muted Kodachrome colors.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the camera's obsession with Carol — the film sees her the way Therese does. Notice how every glance is loaded, because in 1952 a glance could ruin a life.

name: Son of Saul (2015)
teaser: A Jewish prisoner in Auschwitz works in the Sonderkommando, burning the bodies of the dead, and risks everything to give one boy a proper burial. László Nemes's debut films nearly the whole story in tight close-up on its hero's face, with the horrors of the camp blurring in the background. It won the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the shallow focus — the camera never lets you look away from Saul, and never lets you see too much. Notice how the film makes the choice to bury the boy an act of humanity inside hell.

name: Mustang (2015)
teaser: Five orphaned sisters in a Turkish village are locked into their house by their uncle after a game with boys is spotted, and marriage becomes the only exit. Deniz Gamze Ergüven's debut turns a coming-of-age story into a portrait of control. The sisters' escapes and rebellions earned it the Oscar nomination.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the house becomes more prison-like with each scene — bars, locks, curtains. Notice how the sisters' games and secrets are their only freedom.

name: Embrace of the Serpent (2015)
teaser: Two Amazon explorers, eighty years apart, search for a sacred plant with the help of the same dying shaman, and both journeys map the destruction of his world. Ciro Guerra's black-and-white epic, shot in real rainforest, tells the story of colonialism from the inside out. The shaman's grandson is the only thread linking the two expeditions.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the dual timelines — one explorer destroys, the other observes, and the shaman bridges both. Notice how the film refuses to romanticize either the jungle or the men who enter it.

name: The Assassin (2015)
teaser: A trained killer is sent to eliminate a provincial governor — the man she once loved and was promised to — in ninth-century China. Hou Hsiao-hsien's martial-arts film moves with the patience of a landscape painting, each fight over in seconds. It won Best Director at Cannes for its unhurried elegance.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the fights — they are over almost before they begin, the violence compressed into a few frames. Notice how the film's beauty is a weapon too: the silk, the mist, the stillness.

name: Youth (2015)
teaser: An aging composer vacationing in the Alps refuses to conduct for the Queen, while his filmmaker friend works on his last screenplay and the guests around them perform their final acts. Paolo Sorrentino's dreamy meditation stars Michael Caine and Harvey Keitel. The film's images — a floating old man, a walking Vespa — linger long after.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the hotel guests' small stories mirror the two old friends' big ones. Notice how the film treats aging as a performance — one last show where everyone is the star.

name: Legend (2015)
teaser: The Kray twins ran 1960s London's underworld together — identical twins, one charming and one psychopathic — until their brotherhood tore itself apart. Tom Hardy plays both brothers in Brian Helgeland's gangster film. The film mixes the brothers' rise with the violence that finally separated them.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch Hardy play two men in the same frame — the difference is in the eyes and the posture. Notice how the twins' bond is both their strength and their doom.

name: Tangerine (2015)
teaser: A transgender sex worker in Los Angeles learns her boyfriend cheated on her while she was in jail, and she storms across the city with her best friend on Christmas Eve. Sean Baker shot the film entirely on an iPhone, with natural light and real streets. The result is raw, funny, and tender all at once.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the iPhone framing puts you on the sidewalk with the characters. Notice how the film treats its world without pity — the humor and the heart are equal parts.

name: Dope (2015)
teaser: A straight-A geek in Inglewood, California, dreams of escaping to Harvard, but a birthday party gone wrong lands him with a bag of drugs and a choice. Rick Famuyiwa's comedy is a coming-of-age story with a 90s hip-hop heart. The film's smart, fast talk updates the teen comedy for a new generation.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how Malcolm's science-club brain solves gang problems. Notice how the film keeps its optimism even when the world keeps pushing back.

name: The Lobster (2015)
teaser: In a near future, single people are sent to a hotel where they have forty-five days to find a mate — or be turned into the animal of their choice. Colin Farrell stars in Yorgos Lanthimos's deadpan dystopian comedy. The film asks what love is worth when it is enforced by law.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the hotel's rules — everything is logical and everything is absurd. Notice how the film's flat delivery makes the cruelty funnier and the romance stranger.

name: Victoria (2015)
teaser: A young Spanish woman in Berlin meets four men outside a club and agrees to a wild night out that turns into a bank robbery. Sebastian Schipper shot the entire film in one continuous 134-minute take. The single take is not a gimmick — it is the whole experience.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the moment the night tips from fun into danger — the camera never blinks, so neither do you. Notice how the real-time pacing makes the robbery feel inevitable.

name: Anomalisa (2015)
teaser: A customer-service expert who hears everyone as the same voice and face meets a woman whose voice is different, and falls into a brief, strange love. Charlie Kaufman's stop-motion film, with puppets, is the most human movie about loneliness ever animated. It was the first animated film to compete for the Best Picture Oscar.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the hotel-room scene — the film's emotional peak happens between two puppets. Notice how the identical voices make every other character a blur around the one exception.

name: 45 Years (2015)
teaser: A week before their forty-fifth anniversary party, a retired couple learns that the body of the husband's first love has been found frozen in the Alps. Charlotte Rampling won the Silver Bear for a performance built entirely from small silences. The final dance scene is one of cinema's great endings.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how Geoff's memory grows louder while his voice grows quieter. Notice the final scene — the dance, the hand, and the question the film leaves in the air.

name: Amy (2015)
teaser: The rise and fall of Amy Winehouse, told through her own home videos, phone calls, and lyrics, with no talking heads explaining her away. Asif Kapadia's documentary assembles a tragedy the tabloids narrated but never understood. The film ends with the song she was writing about wanting to be remembered.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the archive footage lets Amy speak for herself — the film trusts her voice. Notice how the cameras that loved her success also captured her decline.

name: Cartel Land (2015)
teaser: Two men on opposite sides of the U.S.-Mexico border take on the drug cartels: a vigilante leader in Mexico and an American rancher patrolling the Arizona desert. Matthew Heineman's documentary embeds with both men until the danger becomes the film itself. One of the subjects was later convicted of a weapons offense.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the film refuses to cheer for either vigilante. Notice how the camera keeps rolling through scenes most crews would run from.

name: Heart of a Dog (2015)
teaser: Artist Laurie Anderson turns the death of her dog Lolabelle into a meditation on loss, surveillance, memory, and the afterlife. Her essay film mixes animation, home movies, and her own narration. The film is a eulogy that becomes a philosophy of how we say goodbye.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how Anderson weaves the dog's story into stories about her mother and about 9/11. Notice how the film treats grief as a shape that can be drawn, sung, and played with.

name: Listen to Me Marlon (2015)
teaser: Marlon Brando narrates his own life through a trove of his private audio recordings, from the childhood that shaped him to the fame that isolated him. Stevan Riley's documentary uses hypnosis tapes and home recordings to let the actor analyze himself. The result is the most intimate portrait of a movie star ever assembled.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the self-hypnosis tapes become the film's framing device — Brando examining Brando. Notice how the archive footage is cut to match his own words about his life.

name: The Look of Silence (2014)
teaser: A middle-aged optician discovers that the men who murdered his brother during Indonesia's 1965 anti-communist purge are his neighbors, still powerful and unrepentant. Joshua Oppenheimer's documentary confronts the killers directly, sitting in their homes and asking them to look at the survivor's eyes. It is the companion film to The Act of Killing.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the optician's eye tests become a moral examination — he asks the killers to look closely at what they did. Notice how the film's calm surfaces hide the terror underneath.

name: Meru (2015)
teaser: Three climbers attempt the Shark's Fin route on Meru Peak in the Himalayas — a wall no one has ever climbed — and fail, then return a year later to try again. Jimmy Chin's documentary, co-directed with Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi, is about obsession measured in oxygen tanks. The film turns climbing into a portrait of friendship under pressure.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the first attempt's retreat — the film's most honest moment. Notice how the second attempt is not a triumph but a reconciliation with the mountain.

name: Rams (2015)
teaser: Two estranged brothers in rural Iceland raise prize-winning sheep and have not spoken in forty years, until a government order forces them to slaughter their flocks. Grímur Hákonarson's deadpan drama turns sheep farming into a fable about stubbornness and love. The final shot is both absurd and deeply moving.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the brothers' rivalry is communicated entirely through animals and silence. Notice how the film's ending balances tragedy with a strange, stubborn hope.

name: Theeb (2014)
teaser: A Bedouin boy in 1916 follows his older brother to guide a mysterious English officer through the desert, and the journey turns into a survival test. Naji Abu Nowar's film was shot in the actual Wadi Rum with a cast of non-actors. It won the Best Director award at Venice.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the desert is shot — vast, silent, and indifferent to the boy's fate. Notice how the film slowly turns the coming-of-age story into a thriller of survival.

name: Timbuktu (2014)
teaser: In the Malian city under jihadist occupation, a cattle herder and his family live under a new set of laws enforced by young men with guns and loudspeakers. Abderrahmane Sissako's film shows daily life under extremism with poetry and anger. The penalty for music is whipping; the penalty for love is death.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the football match played without a ball — a small rebellion filmed with tenderness. Notice how the film balances the occupiers' cruelty with their own humanity.

name: Two Days, One Night (2014)
teaser: A factory worker has one weekend to convince her colleagues to give up their bonuses so she can keep her job, one doorstep at a time. Marion Cotillard gives the performance of her career in the Dardenne brothers' moral puzzle. Every vote forces the film's question: what is a person worth?

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the structure — each visit is a small ethical trial. Notice how Sandra's depression and the workers' excuses keep the stakes human rather than abstract.

name: Wild Tales (2014)
teaser: Six short films about ordinary people pushed past their breaking point — a plane full of guests who once wronged the pilot, a bride who discovers her husband's affair at the reception. Damián Szifron's black comedy turns revenge into a genre with six variations. Each story ends in chaos and laughter.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the escalation in each story — every outrage is met with an outrage. Notice how the film's gleeful violence is aimed at the small cruelties of everyday life.

name: The Salt of the Earth (2014)
teaser: Photographer Sebastião Salgado spent four decades documenting workers, migrants, and the destruction of the earth, and then set out to plant a forest. Wim Wenders's documentary lets Salgado's images tell a history of the twentieth century. The final act, replanting a Brazilian valley, turns despair into hope.

exploreAction.targetName: The Salt of the Earth (2014) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the gold mine sequence — thousands of workers on a single hillside, shot like an epic. Notice how Salgado's photographs make the invisible visible, and then how he gives something back.

name: Citizenfour (2014)
teaser: Filmmaker Laura Poitras was in a Hong Kong hotel room when Edward Snowden revealed the scale of global surveillance, and her camera was rolling. The documentary is a real-time record of a whistleblower's gamble. It won the Oscar for Best Documentary Feature.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the hotel room scenes — the film's tension is the world watching through the same door. Notice how the film lets Snowden's own words carry the argument.

name: Leviathan (2014)
teaser: A man in a small Russian coastal town fights the corrupt mayor who wants his land, and the machinery of the state grinds him down. Andrey Zvyagintsev's film, shot with a whale skeleton looming over the town, is a modern retelling of the Book of Job. The land is Russia itself.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the courtroom and church scenes — institutions failing the same man. Notice how the film's bleakness is interrupted by moments of dark humor that make it bearable.

name: Ida (2013)
teaser: A young novitiate in 1960s Poland learns she is Jewish and that her parents were murdered, and she goes searching for the truth with her cynical, beautiful aunt. Paweł Pawlikowski's film is shot in austere black and white with the figures low in the frame. It won the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the framing — characters occupy the bottom of the frame, leaving vast empty space above them. Notice how the film's silence and stillness carry the weight of the Holocaust.

name: A Most Violent Year (2014)
teaser: A rising trucking magnate in 1981 New York tries to run an honest business while hijackers, unions, and prosecutors squeeze him from every side. J.C. Chandor's slow-burn crime drama stars Oscar Isaac and Jessica Chastain. The violence the title promises mostly stays off-screen — which makes it scarier.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the moments of restraint — the film's power is in what it refuses to show. Notice how the heroine's steel and the hero's principles make them a dangerous pair.

name: American Sniper (2014)
teaser: Navy SEAL Chris Kyle became the most lethal sniper in American military history, and the war he carried home was the one that nearly killed him. Clint Eastwood's film is both a tribute and a portrait of a man who could not leave Iraq behind. The shooting range scene with the child is its most haunting moment.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the film splits between Kyle's two wars — the desert and the home front. Notice how the rules-of-engagement dilemma sets up every choice he makes.

name: It Follows (2014)
teaser: A teenager who has sex with the wrong boy is cursed: a shapeshifting presence will follow her forever, walking slowly, until she passes it on to someone else. David Robert Mitchell's horror film turns the sex-death link of the genre into a literal rule. The film's sense of dread is built from patient, wide shots.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the figure in the background — it is always there, just walking. Notice how the film's retro look makes the threat feel timeless rather than dated.

name: The Babadook (2014)
teaser: A widowed mother and her difficult son are haunted by a monster from a pop-up book that may be grief itself. Jennifer Kent's debut builds its horror from the exhaustion of single parenthood. The film became an unexpected symbol for mental illness and queerness — though its director never planned either reading.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the monster and the mother's breakdown become the same story. Notice how the film's sound design makes the house itself feel like it is screaming.

name: Under the Skin (2013)
teaser: An alien in human form drives through Glasgow picking up men, and what she does with them is stranger than murder. Scarlett Johansson plays the predator who slowly discovers what it means to be human. Jonathan Glazer's film is almost wordless, almost plotless, and unforgettable.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the seduction scenes — filmed with hidden cameras and real men who did not know they were being filmed. Notice how the film's black mirror room is where identity dissolves.

name: Nebraska (2013)
teaser: A delusional old man believes he has won a million dollars in a magazine sweepstakes, and his long-suffering son agrees to drive him across the Midwest to collect. Alexander Payne shot the film in black and white, with Bruce Dern and a great deadpan Will Forte. The family scenes are tender and brutal in the same breath.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the scenes with Woody's old friends and relatives — the film's small-town portrait is its real subject. Notice how the prize matters less than what the trip gives the two men.

name: Philomena (2013)
teaser: A retired Irish nurse spends fifty years searching for the son she was forced to give up in a convent, and a cynical journalist helps her find him. Judi Dench's Philomena and Steve Coogan's Martin Sixsmith make an odd couple on a road of secrets. The film is about forgiveness that does not require forgetting.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how Philomena's faith survives every revelation — she forgives what the audience cannot. Notice how the convent's coldness is never exaggerated; it is simply recorded.

name: The Great Beauty (2013)
teaser: An aging writer who wrote one great novel fifty years ago drifts through Rome's parties, rooftops, and ruins, searching for the beauty he once promised to describe. Paolo Sorrentino's visual symphony won the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film. The opening party scene is a festival of excess that sets the film's whole tone.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the party scenes — the camera glides through them like a swimmer. Notice how the film's beauty is both the subject and the trap: Rome is gorgeous and empty.

name: The Master (2012)
teaser: A drifting, violent navy veteran falls under the spell of a charismatic cult leader who claims he can heal the mind. Paul Thomas Anderson's film is a study of the relationship between a man who wants to be controlled and a man who wants to control. Philip Seymour Hoffman and Joaquin Phoenix trade the film's best scenes.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the processing scene — the film's famous interrogation where the two men find each other. Notice how Anderson leaves the cult's beliefs vague so the power struggle stays central.

name: Arbitrage (2012)
teaser: A billionaire hedge-fund king covers up a fatal accident just as a suspicious deal is collapsing, and his whole empire starts to slide. Richard Gere gives one of his best performances as a man who believes his own lies. The film is a portrait of the 2008 collapse told through one arrogant survivor.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how Miller's genius and his recklessness are the same trait. Notice how the film refuses to punish its hero — the point is that men like him walk away.

name: Holy Motors (2012)
teaser: A man in a white limousine drives through Paris playing a dozen different roles a day — assassin, beggar, monster, father — each performance witnessed by an audience of one. Leos Carax's surreal masterpiece is a love letter to cinema itself, ending with a conversation between talking limousines. Denis Lavant plays every part with total commitment.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how each appointment is a mini-film with its own genre and rules. Notice how the film asks who we are when every identity is a performance.

name: The Hunt (2012)
teaser: A kindergarten teacher in a close-knit Danish town is accused of abuse by a child whose lie he cannot disprove, and the community turns on him with quiet, total certainty. Mads Mikkelsen gives the performance of his career as a man whose innocence makes him the perfect target. The film is a study of how easily a life can be destroyed.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the accusation spreads — a rumor moving through a village with perfect social logic. Notice the supermarket scene, where the film's whole point lands without a single raised voice.

name: A Royal Affair (2012)
teaser: In eighteenth-century Denmark, a young English queen falls in love with the king's personal physician, and together the lovers try to drag a mad king's court into the Enlightenment. Mads Mikkelsen, Alicia Vikander, and the film's real history earned it an Oscar nomination for Best Foreign Language Film. The affair changed a nation.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the romance and the revolution advance together — the doctor's reforms are acts of love. Notice how the film balances candlelit intimacy with the machinery of power.

name: Rififi (1955)
teaser: Four French gangsters plan the perfect jewel heist: silence, discipline, and a locked safe that takes half an hour to crack. Jules Dassin, blacklisted in Hollywood, made the film in exile, and its famous heist sequence — played without a word of dialogue — became the template for every heist film since. The crime goes flawlessly; everything after does not.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the thirty-minute heist — no dialogue, no music, only the mechanics of the job. Notice how the film's title, slang for a brawl, becomes a warning about what happens when greed wins.
